newsitem.title: USA: Pacificare reports sharply lower second quarter.
newsitem.headline: Pacificare reports sharply lower second quarter.

text.p: PacifiCare Health Systems Inc. Thursday reported a sharp drop in second-quarter earnings, citing rising drug costs and problems integrating the newly acquired FHP International Co.

The company, which first warned of a steep shortfall in June, said it considers the results unacceptable, but believes it has identified the source of most of its problems and has started to turn itself around.

PacifiCare, the fifth-largest health maintenance organisation in the United States, said its earnings totalled $18 million, or 39 cents per share, in the period. A year earlier, its earnings from operations were $36 million, or $1.15 per share. However an extraordinary charge took net earnings to $8.6 million, or 27 cents per share, in the 1996 quarter.
Second-quarter revenues rose to $2.38 billion from $1.19 billion.
PacifiCare stock was down 50 cents at $64.375 on Nasdaq, around a level it fell to in June after the earnings warning triggered a sell-off.

The problems contributing to PacifiCare's weak quarter were wide-ranging, including inflated drug costs coupled with a competitive price environment, the company said. Like many health care providers, PacifiCare gave up profits by keeping its premiums low so it could compete for new membership.
The company also said it underestimated the extent of problems at FHP, where operations in some markets were generating virtually no profit.
Analysts who spoke with company officials said PacifiCare is shifting its strategy to raise premiums and sacrifice some new membership.
Volpe Welty analyst Ed Keaney said the company forecast membership growth in the near term would drop to the low to mid-single digit range, down from past growth in the mid-teens or low-twenties.
Keaney said there was "no question" PacifiCare's approach was correct. "I think they've been burned pretty badly in the past by not raising prices," he said.
He added that PacifiCare forecast in a conference call with analysts that it could return profit margins to their historical level around 3.5 percent, from its current 1.8 percent, by 1998.
"They're focusing on profitable growth and giving up some on the enrollments side," said Bear Stearns analyst Gary Frazier. "In this era it makes a lot of sense to focus on managing margins."
